newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa pitches for Zaire talks on Saturday.
newsitem.headline: South Africa pitches for Zaire talks on Saturday.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela, host to on-off Zaire peace talks at sea, will make a fresh attempt on Saturday to bring ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila together.

"We optimistically hope that sometime tomorrow it will start," South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad told reporters on board the converted icebreaker SAS Outeniqua after Kabila failed to show for the talks on Friday.

He said Mandela, who sailed into international waters with Mobutu for the talks rendezvous, would probably spend the night on the South African naval ship and was willing to stay on in the hope of the talks getting under way on Saturday. "He feels he has to stay," Pahad said.
Kabila shunned the seaborne summit on Friday, remaining in Angola's capital Luanda.
"I will go to the ship tomorrow if I receive adequate assurances from the South Africans tomorrow that security arrangements are in place," he told a news conference.
"If we wanted to we could win this militarily in two weeks. Suggestions that I am stalling for time are ridiculous. I am interested in finding a peaceful solution to the problem."

Mobutu, who is 66 and suffering from prostate cancer, left the Outeniqua in Congo's port of Pointe Noire late on Friday. Pahad said Mobutu would stay the night there with Congo's president, Pascal Lissouba.
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October and now control around three quarters of Zaire, mustered in force at Kikwit on the road to Kinshasa and pressed on with their march on the capital.
Mobutu has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965 but his illness and the whirlwind rebel offensive have weakened his grip on the former Belgian colony.
He is one of Africa's most enduring strongmen and was backed by the United States during the Cold War as a bulwark against Soviet communism.
Mobutu boarded the Russian-built Outeniqua in Pointe Noire with great difficulty on Friday. Unable to climb 31 steep steps, he was driven on board five hours late up a make-shift ramp.
His aides say the talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. They reject suggestions that the meeting is a face-saver to allow him to stand down with dignity.

Kabila, 56, says Mobutu must go and has refused to declare a truce for the talks. "There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," he said on Wednesday.

A commander at rebel headquarters in the southeastern city of Lubumbashi said an airlift of rebels and equipment to the towns of Kikwit and Kanaga began on Thursday and rebel forces were about to enter Kenge, 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson, who has been helping Mandela bring the two sides together, has said there are no conditions for the talks.
"In my view this meeting will produce a process that involves a transfer of power and hopefully a transitional, inclusive government," he said on Friday.
Diplomats see the talks as a last chance to avert a bloody battle for Zaire's capital of five million people.
The United States, France, Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo's capital Brazzaville to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
